utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We have an application before us by the Prosecutor to call new evidence. May we hear if there is any objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are objections and the defence of Mr. Delalic has provided its objections to the Prosecutor's office as requested. We are gathered here today upon your order in order to hear the arguments regarding this motion by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mrs. McHenry, can we hear you on your motion then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I am not going to go over what has already been set forth in our motion. What I would like to do today is just to briefly summarise some of what is set out in our motion and then to answer any questions the Chamber might have. In brief, the Prosecution seeks to introduce three brief witnesses to introduce a limited number of documents recently obtained by the Prosecution. I believe one of the first questions that comes up is, are the documents relevant? It is clear, I think, from any review of the documents that they are of direct relevance to a number of issues that have arisen in these proceedings. They are of crucial importance and, indeed, the Defence, I do not hear to argue that the documents are not extremely relevant to the matters before Your Honour. A second question is, did the Prosecution make reasonable efforts to obtain the documents prior to closing its case? In our motion we have described just some of the efforts and they are so numerous that I will not bother going through them each in detail. But certainly, the evidence, the record indicates that we attempted to obtain all relevant documents from a number of witnesses and from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Finally, the Prosecution did resort to requesting and obtaining search warrants, which assisted us in finally obtaining a number of the documents. And really, another question is, will the introduction of these documents unfairly prejudice the Defence? And again, the Prosecution submits that the answer is clearly no. Indeed, I don't see the Defence to argue that they are prejudiced. Any sort of slight prejudice that might be suffered can be remedied by allowing them to call additional evidence if necessary, given the limited scope of the material that the Prosecution seeks to introduce that would not require a lengthy delay in this trial. The Prosecution submits that overall the question is, will the documents, the additional evidence, aid this Chamber in arriving at the truth and in arriving at justice in these proceedings? And when you look at all the circumstances, the Prosecution submits that the answer must be yes, that these documents will aid, the truth finding process will aid the reaching of justice in this case and will not in any way result in an unfair trial to the accused. To the contrary, it will result in a fair trial to everyone involved. Unless Your Honours have any specific factual questions or any question that I might assist, I believe the other specifics are set forth in our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I go to the other microphone because I seem to be having some technical difficulties with the headphones here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must make it clear straight away what my position is regarding the comment of my learned colleague, Ms. McHenry, by saying that the Defence emphatically deems that at this point in time there is no cause to discuss the relevance of evidence, nor does it consider that regarding the position of Zejnil Delalic, the offered documents have any relevance. I also wish to state at the outset that the re-opening of the case, as opposed to the understanding for the position of the Defence shown by my colleague, are indeed harmful to the position of my defendant and imply a direct violation of the rights envisaged by Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute. In my written response filed at the request of the Prosecution, with the Court on the 31st of July, '98, we have referred Your Honours to only those issues which have any significance and which warrant the raising of the question of the re-opening of the case because of alleged new evidence. In that regard, we were guided by the position of this Trial Chamber, which was quite clearly stated on the 24th of July, when it instructed the Prosecutor to provide valid reasons as to whether it has invested sufficient effort in these proceedings which have been going on, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, since 1995, in order to obtain this evidence in a timely fashion and to produce them in court. That is why I shall refer very briefly to what we said in our written response. But in my oral argument I should like to focus on Chapter 4, which the Prosecution, without any legal grounds, has introduced into the proceedings at this stage claiming that the question of the re-opening of the criminal proceedings after the termination of the case of the Prosecution and the Defence that the relevance of the new evidence is of primary importance. The position of Delalic's Defence is as follows: First, at a session on the 24th of July, a representative of the Prosecution orally made the request that it be allowed to re-open the case on the basis of new evidence. We submit that this Trial Chamber ruled at the time regarding this oral request. Secondly, the Prosecutor has not met the legal criteria required for the re-opening of the case, nor has she proven that she has undertaken reasonable measures in order to gain possession of the evidence prior to the completion of the presentation of its own evidence on the 16th of February, 1998. And thirdly, the Prosecutor, contrary to the criteria questions put to it by the Trial Chamber has introduced in this Chamber the question of the alleged relevance of the newly obtained evidence. With regard to the first question as we have stated in our written submission, we feel that the Court has decided on the 24th of July, that it is not possible to present evidence through the testimony of Rajko Dordic, Stephen Chambers because this is new evidence and then it has also ruled that the question of new evidence cannot be raised. This Chamber has also ruled that Professor Stegnar cannot testify because the question of her expert opinion and report has already been determined by this Trial Chamber as well as by the appellate, Appeals Chamber. Opposition has clearly been stated earlier on and also in our written response to the Prosecutor's request to re-open the case. We submit that legal causes are required for the re-opening of the case as stated by this Trial Chamber on the 24th of July. That is that the Prosecutor is obliged to show that he has taken all reasonable steps to obtain the evidence, the witnesses or documents, prior to the conclusion of its case on the 16th of February, 1998. Mr. President, you, yourself, have specifically indicated the criteria that need to be met and those criteria can be found in the transcript on pages 14.950 and 14.972. Any different action would be contrary to the provisions of an expeditious and fair trial as envisaged by Articles 20 and 21 of the Court's Statute. Wishing to provide grounds for the Trial Chamber for it to be able to rely on decisions of other Trial Chambers of this Court. In its request, the Prosecutor has cited decisions in the Kovacevic and Furundzija cases, neither of which in the position of the Defence has any connection with the legal issue before this Trial Chamber. In this way, an intent is being made to assert that there is a precedent in this Court along these lines. However, in the Kovacevic case, it was a question of amending the indictment in the pre-trial proceedings and at a time when the accused had spent only ten months in detention. In our case, the legal issue of re-opening the case is being raised when both the Prosecution and the Defence cases have been completed and after almost a year and a half since the beginning of the trial and almost two and a half years since the accused have been in detention. The legal and actual facts regarding the Furundzija case are clearly quite different and this is something that we have explained in our written submission. I should just like to add on this occasion that those issues were raised after the accused had spent only six months in detention. The Prosecutor in its request could not confirm that the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not cooperate with her. Attached to our response are Annexes 1 A and B, containing the statements of our learned colleague Mr. Niemann before this Trial Chamber regarding the proposal for a subpoena; the statement of our learned colleague, Ms. McHenry when witness Mr. Omerkic was testifying and also memos exchanged between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Prosecution. It is also clear that the Prosecution and we always bore in mind Articles 29 of the Statute and if the Prosecutor encountered any problem in the area of cooperation with competent authorities, it had a possibility to request assistance from the Trial Chamber. I should like you, Your Honours, that you, yourself, during the Defence case did on a number of occasions, draw attention to this article of the statute, indicating the consequences for the Defence if it does not request the assistance of the Trial Chamber on time. The Prosecutor also asserts that it did not have any police forces at its disposal and we wish to add that the testimony of the Prosecution witness, Regis Abribat, stated that since the spring of '95, twelve investigators were conducting investigations in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that also since '96, the Prosecutor had a standing office in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That it also had at its disposal other instruments. And, more recently, the possibility of eliciting the cooperation of the S-4 forces. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber rightly indicated to the Prosecutor that these were state institutions. That these institutions exist for many years. And that given greater effort, a higher degree of efficiency, it could have been possible to review the archives in a timely fashion when this would have been in the interest of an expeditious and fair trial. It can be seen from the Prosecutor's motion itself that it has been collaborating with state institutions for three years now. And, for two and a half years, it has had contacts with a person who, according to her allegations, did not disclose certain documents. It failed to take any steps to summon a witness or to gain possession of the necessary documents. As anyone coming to this Court knows Jasna Dorko -- Jasmin Kajunhor (Phoen), then it is very strange that the Prosecutor should have learned of her address only two months ago. And also strange that the Prosecution did not request assistance from the Court, a subpoena or any other kind of relief from the Court to help it in obtaining evidence which it may have been considered to be relevant. In connection with the testimony of Rajko Dordic, in our previous motion, when we opposed the rebuttal, we presented sufficient arguments at the hearing of the 24th of July, as well as arguments regarding the testimony of Professor Stegnar. Therefore, Mr. Delalic's Defence counsel is very explicit in opposing the re-opening of the case and a further continuation of proceedings because, as we have pointed out in responding to the new schedule of the Trial Chamber, a re-opening of the case would mean a significant prolongation of the proceedings and a serious threat to the rights of the accused under Articles 20 and 21. In the event of re-opening, the Prosecutor would have to present new evidence and prove all the elements of that evidence. The Defence would necessarily have the right to undertake certain investigations to verify that evidence and then to present its own evidence. In that case, the Prosecutor would be entitled to a rebuttal case and then the Defence again would have the right to a rejoinder. Let me just say that quite recently the Prosecutor has disclosed this to us, not only what it has provided you with, but all this evidence, which, given a more detailed review, could fully reject this evidence that is being proposed. A very brief and superficial verification of the place from where this documentation was taken has given us indication to believe that though we did ask the Prosecutor to provide us with all the documents seized there. We have not been given an all the documents. But, on the other hand, we were given documents that were not at all found there, but elsewhere. Therefore, this kind of re-opening would require proceedings which would last several weeks, maybe even months in order to review any possible new evidence in terms of its authenticity, its probative value and its relevance. May I now be allowed, Your Honours, to comment on Part 4 of the Prosecutor's request? I have already referred to the criteria and the requirements made by the Trial Chamber to the Prosecution on the 24th of July. But in this request, the Prosecutor, in Chapter 4 reviews the relevance of the documents. Relying partly also on the question of the admissibility of evidence according to the civil law system and the Prosecutor feels that this is decisive for your decision. In addition to the request in which it describes the documents and assesses them as if they had already been presented in court, the Prosecutor, this time, discloses to the Court all the documents it has in mind. We have been in the proceedings for a year and a half and the Trial Chamber has guided us and taught us as to proper procedure. But it seems to us that this is not in line with that proper procedure for the proceedings to be fair and expeditious and in line with the Statute. I am not trying to say this if such a procedure were not be adopted, then a Trial Chamber could ask the parties before starting a trial for them to submit all possible documents for it to assess its relevance and only then to start the trial. This kind of legal procedure and actual approach to the examination of any evidence, in my opinion, is not acceptable and Mr. Delalic's Defence will try to influence the Trial Chamber to rule in a different manner. However, even though we feel that the documents proposed do not have the relevance or probative value that could change the position of our client, I will, being forced to react by the list of documents given by the Prosecution, I shall have to comment on a part of those documents. As the Prosecutor relies on the legal experiences and legal practices of various legal systems, may I remind Your Honours that you too have examined these issues and ruled on two occasions. Once, when a decision had to be taken on the admission of Exhibit 155 into evidence and the request of the Prosecution to be ordered to submit an example of his handwriting on the 19th of January and regarding the decision to admit certain evidence. That is, the Vienna document of the same date. In both cases, Your Honours, you reviewed in detail the question of relevance, reliability and probative value. In both rulings, analysing various national systems of the civil law and common law systems, you took the position that the concept of relevance implicitly contains the demand for the existence of probative value. As a lawyer active in criminal law in a civil law system, the question of relevance in this stage of the proceedings, that is new evidence, it is very restrictively interpreted in law in general and it contains inherently the need for two substantive elements. First, to prove that this is new subsequently found evidence which is in no way the fault of the party offering it. And, secondly, that this subsequently found evidence has such probative value that it can result in a completely different view of your already established facts. By way of example, a situation that may lead to acquittal or, on the other hand, that may lead to sentencing when the previous impression was the opposite. Therefore, procedural law, when assessing the relevance of new evidence, focuses on the main elements of the charges made against an accused, and only if it can result in a substantive change of the position of the accused can it be considered new and acceptable. The Defence of Delalic deems that not one of the documents offered is such evidence whereby things that have already been said cannot be considered new evidence or relevant evidence. And I should like to remind you, Your Honours, of the fact that during the presentation of evidence by the Defence, you cautioned me repeatedly that the presentation of new evidence about facts which have already been testified to, that is, that the multiplication of evidence does not affect its probative value, nor its relevance. In the position of Mr. Delalic's defence, the documents described by the Prosecution, Chapter 4, page 11, from A to Z, is considered by us to be totally irrelevant for this case. And the position of the Prosecution in point 46 would mean just multiplication of numerous evidence presented regarding the status of detainees in Celebici. Therefore, numerous repeated evidence regarding the status of prisoners, which is a legal issue, and about which only this Trial Chamber can rule. The documents listed in the same chapter by the Prosecutor on page 11, point 45, C to F, even if they were authentic, would be totally irrelevant. They do not refer to the points in the indictment and have no significance for the position of the accused, and particularly not for the position of Mr. Delalic. The document referred to on point 45 F, presented by the Prosecution during the Defence case and shown to one of the Defence witnesses, regardless of the fact that it is not authentic or reliable, it is not even relevant. Because if the Prosecutor felt that it was relevant, then it would have tendered it to the Court as relevant evidence in line with Rule 89 C and would have proposed it into evidence as it has done on a number of occasions during this trial. As for items 48 and 49 of the request, the Prosecutor describes and alleges the relevance of an allegedly found letter of Zejnil Delalic. At this point in time I do not wish to go into it, as there is a Court ruling regarding material found in a similar fashion; but I wish to say that by commenting on this document and trying to prove its relevance, the Prosecutor himself interprets the letter on the basis of hearsay, what the investigator told the Prosecutor, and a third person to the Prosecutor, and then somebody else. This letter, too, is in no way related to the charges in the indictment and the position of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Maybe from the standpoint of interference with a witness it could be relevant, but even this fact is not mentioned here; because the person identified on whom allegedly this letter was found was never a witness on the Prosecutor's list or on the Defence list. The document referred to on point 50 I is not relevant and has no probative value for the charges in the indictment. It simply confirms that some documents authored by the Prosecution were in the possession of the State Commission in Sarajevo since February, '97. And in view of the cooperation between the Prosecutor and the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if the Prosecutor had been diligent it could have gained possession of those documents. Delalic's defence simply cannot understand that an unsigned document dated the 30th of May '92, can be offered as a relevant piece of evidence. In point 55 of its request, the Prosecutor refers, attaches this document to Mr. Delalic, although he is not mentioned in it. The document is not signed, and if we were to assess it in terms of the names typed by a typewriter, we could find the name of the commander of the TO, the commander of the HVO, the chief of police and the coordinator of combat formations. There is absolutely no name attached to that position. The evidence presented in Court has clearly shown so far that Mr. Delalic has absolutely no connection with the coordinators of combat units, nor did he ever hold such a position. We knew, we know who was the coordinator of the battles in Bradina, in the operation Oganj and other operations, but it was never Zejnil Delalic. Therefore, its relevance from the standpoint of this trial, as an unsigned form that has no connection with any of the accused, is absolutely irrelevant. The document on H is also irrelevant because it reviews questions of the exchange of prisoners, and the question of exchange of prisoners are not described in any of the points of the indictment. Not only does the Prosecutor have to prove the chain of custody and its authenticity, from the standpoint of the responsibility of Mr. Delalic it has no relevance, because the superior authority and control over guards has nothing to do with the exchange of prisoners. The document mentioned on point 50 L is also quite irrelevant from the standpoint of the responsibility of Mr. Delalic in point 7 of the indictment. Even if the authenticity of this document were to be proven, this would just be one in a series of documents and testimony that this Trial Chamber has already heard, that the tactical group was used for the transfer of information because it was in the immediate vicinity of Sarajevo. That is, tactical groups were used for the transfer of information between certain bodies in Sarajevo and municipal authorities in Konjic. The document referred to on item 50 M also cannot be considered new evidence for the already mentioned reasons, because it was agreed on the 28th of August -- because it was dated 28th of August '92, and it shows that the coordinator of the tactical group transferred orders from Sarajevo to local authorities. Documents 50 N and O also cannot be considered relevant because even if they were authentic and reliable, they are multiplication of previously presented evidence on interrogation records and release documents. We have seen witnesses released in this way, we have seen videotapes, and a part, a set of such documents presented in Court. The documents referred to under 52 P and Q also cannot be considered new evidence because this Trial Chamber has had a number of witnesses of the Prosecution and the Defence regarding Zeljko Klimenta and the Prosecutor, pursuant to its obligations under Rule 66, submitted to the Defence already in '96 a statement of the person who caused the death of Zeljko Klimenta. And this fact was known to the Prosecutor in 1996 and, therefore, cannot be considered as new evidence. If this fact had been relevant for the Prosecution, it could have presented it in Court earlier on. The document under 52 R would also be a multiplication of evidence showing that even the commander of the prison didn't have knowledge as to the real cause of death of individual persons. And evidence has been presented in Court, the certificates of the standard enterprise, its employee, the statements of Dr. Petko Grubac and other witnesses; so I don't wish to dwell on this at length. This is not new evidence, but a document which would be multiplication of evidence already presented. Regarding Zejnil Delalic and documents under 52 Q and R have no relevance to his position or responsibility for the charges contained in the indictment. The document referred to in point 52 S is commented on by the Prosecutor in 54 and 49, claiming that it shows position of authority over the Celebici prison and is linked to the statement of Hazim Delic of 19th of July. This is a photocopy of a document, and in connection with it, the Defence of Zejnil Delalic wishes to state that it has no connection with the position of Mr. Delalic, and at the same time it objects to the interpretation made by the Prosecution for the following reason: First, the Prosecution, without any basis, contrary to the decision of this Trial Chamber takes advantage of a statement of one of the accused against another. Furthermore, it uses this statement in an inadequate manner, citing only parts of that statement, neglecting to mention that even in that statement Hazim Delic clearly responded to a specific question that with regard to a particular document he was not present when that document was signed by Zejnil Delalic. That document in itself is contradictory. A photocopy is not an authentic or reliable document, and it was found, according to the Prosecutor, in places with which Zejnil Delalic has no physical or professional connections. Even if there were a signature on such a document, it would be the signature of a witness of the take-over of the document and not of the person actually issuing it. Regarding the interpretation of this statement of the accused Delic, we want to point out that the same accused gave a very different interpretation in his other statement of July '97, and the Prosecution has not taken into account how these statements were changing over a period of time. Also, in assessing this statement as, this document, as to its reliability, it cannot be accepted; and if we should look at it from the standpoint of our own practice here at this Tribunal regarding its relevance and its potential value as a new document, it is obvious that no new facts can be reached from this statement, which includes Divjak statement, Olujic, Pasalic and other numerous documents which all point to who had command responsibility over the prison, and then a number of documents which again point out that Mr. Delalic had no authority over the prison and the guards therein all the way down to the last witness who testified in that regard, which was the witness of the accused Landzo who had, who was fully protected, but it was a witness who sent the guards from his unit and who confirmed before this Trial Chamber who had the authority over the guards there. In any event, it was not Zejnil Delalic. In other words, no documents which relevance is being sought by the Prosecution are not relevant with respect to the practice of this Trial Chamber and this legal system, and in that respect they cannot be perceived as new and relevant. Therefore, we believe that the Prosecution could not even have raised this issue, and once having raised it, that they have not supported it by any documents which should induce this Trial Chamber to change its position and reopen this case. Your Honours, let me point out again that my client has been detained since 18 March 1996, and that his psychological capacity to withstand continuation of these proceedings will be a real test. And also, we want to point out that the Defence does not appreciate being put in a position to have to argue the relevance of documents which have clearly been produced, which have not been produced as relevant documents at all. We also say that Mr. Zejnil Delalic has absolutely no relation to any of the charges stemming from these newly offered documents, and therefore, we believe that it is not relevant for the indictment itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is Mr. Olujic making any contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with your permission I will be much briefer in comparison to my learned colleague. With respect to the motion of the Prosecution of the 30th of July of this year, and I must say that a lot of effort was put into this motion in order to reach what we call the reopening of the trial, the main trial hearing. The Defence of Mr. Mucic will only highlight some of the arguments already set forth by my learned colleague, and let me enumerate them. Number one, let me point out that any reference to other precedent in other cases, let me point out that each case is unique, and that the very need to bring new witnesses on the part of the Prosecution needs to be previously tested and proven. This has not been done in this particular case, and therefore, can be considered irrelevant. Regarding the experts which the Prosecution is asking to investigate: They could have been brought forth previously, and by analysing their statements we have not reached a single new fact in these proceedings for which these new witnesses could or should be relevant. We would also like to point out and I believe the Trial Chamber is aware of this, the Prosecution had ample time, more time and more resources for their own investigation and anything else that they used in the presentation of their evidence. If you will, they had more investigators, and it has also produced more witnesses than the Defence did. Thirdly, Your Honours, this is a criminal case during which all of the accused have been in detention. And the Prosecution has literally had years in order to investigate this case, and what can we say to such a Prosecution which now is asking yet additional time for it? Given the information and the reasoning are really not very convincing, and they are not legally relevant for the outcome of these proceedings; in other words, none of these documents cannot contribute to this case to all the information that we have already reached during these proceedings. So, in order not to belabour the point, my, I move, Your Honours, to reject the motion of the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite briefly, all good things have to come to an end. And Judge Jan promised me a year ago I would be home for Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was going to say you didn't mention which Christmas. I noticed we have the distinguished visitor Mr. Ostberg here, and March 10th of last year he stood up at that podium and made his opening statement, which was about a week short of a year from the time the indictment was returned. At some point this thing has to end. If the Trial Chamber is going to find my client innocent, he needs to be out of jail and home. If the Trial Chamber is going to find my client is guilty of some or all of the counts with which he is charged, my client has a right to know how much of the rest of his life he's going to spend in prison. It's time to end this thing. The Prosecution's had plenty of time, they should have had enough evidence to prove their indictment beyond a reasonable doubt in March, 1996 when they returned the indictment and ordered these defendants arrested. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any contribution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Esad Landzo is in agreement with the other Defence counsel and goes along with what's been said here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any replies by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and my reply will be brief, although, if Your Honours wish me to go through the documents one by one, or various efforts one by one, I will do that. Otherwise, I will respond very briefly. Just, I think, to clarify maybe a couple of misunderstandings that may have come up with Defence counsel. One is with respect to the expert witness, it is the case that some evidence that she would be prepared to give is not new evidence, but Your Honours have already ruled that is not rebuttal and we would not intend to ask her questions about that material. Her evidence would be very brief and would be limited to the documents recently obtained by the Prosecution. I thought maybe one Defence counsel had a misunderstanding. Similarly, with respect to the investigators the Prosecution never stated that it had no investigators. The issue with respect to something that was said with respect to search warrants is that the Tribunal's investigators are not, as in normal police cases, armed; so their ability to do, for instance, forcible entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But can be armed. Rule 54.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I can't speak to that specifically. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can be armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And then, finally, just with respect to Mrs. Residovic pointing out that multiplication of testimony does not in and of itself make something true. We would certainly agree with that, but these are not other witnesses who are just going to repeat what other witnesses have said. These are witnesses who will introduce documents from 1992 itself, usually signed by the accused themselves, for matters that are directly relevant. And finally, just again to emphasise that this will not unduly delay the proceedings. It is something that we know is of concern to everyone, including us. The scope of the testimony would be limited, we would be prepared to start tomorrow and it would not delay the proceedings inordinately. And certainly when you compare any sort of test to see how much this would aid the Tribunal in reaching Justice, any minimal delay we would submit acceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, before you sit down, what actually were your fears before you wanted to introduce these documents? Which areas of it do you think are not supported before you needed this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, when Your Honour says properly supported, the Prosecution is not stating that it had no evidence or that it is insufficient evidence for Your Honours to find guilt. The Prosecution is certainly stating, though, however, with respect to a number of issues, and let me just pick out a couple, with respect to whether or not Mr. Delalic had authority, any authority over Celebici when he was coordinator. There is a document signed by Mr. Delalic as coordinator directing that certain people, it's an order from Mr. Delalic to the head of the prison that, I believe, certain people should be released. Similarly, the document with respect to the hand over of authority, for instance, the document dated November 17th, specifically indicates that Mr. Delalic, among other things, appointed, as tactical group one commander, officially appointed the commander of the prison. So, although I would not want to say there is no evidence whatsoever, the Prosecution certainly believes these documents give very specific evidence about some of the contested issues in this trial, and therefore would be of great assistance to Your Honours in understanding the truth about what was happening in 1992 and coming up with a just verdict. If Your Honours would like, I can go through more documents specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think you might. Of course, that is the business for which you wanted new evidence to be introduced, to justify why you are introducing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the, some of the first documents, which would include documents A through F, at least, these documents, among other things, are directly relevant to, one, the prisoner of war status of the accused; and two, at least with respect to one of the documents, discusses the fact that Tactical Group 1 had authority over Celebici prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You know why I asked this question? Your additional or new evidence which you have now suggested appears to have implicit in it the idea that you knew your investigation was not exhausted at the time you brought the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, certainly the Prosecution would not be suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because these things you are now trying to adduce are matters supplementary to all the other evidence you have suggested before, additional to what you have done before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, and the Prosecution, in fact, the Prosecution would point to the fact that these documents are not raising new issues that no one has thought about before, as proof both of how directly relevant they are, and as an indication of how the accused will not be prejudiced by their introduction. But what they are is extremely relevant evidence, documents from 1992, the time at issue, which speak to the issues that are being disputed in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You were aware of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at least with respect to one of these documents, we were aware of its existence because Mr. Delic, for instance, talked about it, and the Prosecution had undergone significant efforts to try to obtain this document, and other documents. Certainly it is the case that the Prosecution believes and still believes that there are relevant documents, and the Defence actually in their Defence case had some, and these are some. But these are particularly relevant documents that help Your Honours and the fact finding function of Your Honours with respect to the disputed issues. So, we're not saying that there is no evidence whatsoever, but we are saying that these documents, which we tried to obtain all relevant documents and have been for a long time; but without going into great detail, there are difficulties in obtaining evidence for all cases before the Tribunal. In this case, the Prosecution did exercise diligence and acted reasonably and recently obtained these documents which go in some cases to the very heart of the matter. We would say that the Defence is not prejudiced by their introduction and that they will assist Your Honours in this Tribunal in reaching a just verdict.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour. How did you obtain these documents now and not four years ago?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that with respect to most of the documents, they were ultimately obtained after the Prosecution obtained a search warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why was not a search warrant obtained earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For, among other things, just one, the Prosecution had been trying, certainly before a search warrant is requested. The Prosecution wants to take all reasonable efforts before it seeks that extraordinary measure. Here, we had requests, both oral, both written and then official requests for assistance under the Tribunal Statute to the Bosnia government asking for all relevant documents and then follow up requests, specifically, for instance, asking that all members of previous commissions, including Jasna turn over all documents. I would also point out that a search warrant is an extraordinary measure, especially in this situation where there is always the possibility for violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, are you suggesting that even by the time you started your case against the accused persons, you still did consider it is time to have issued a search warrant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When did you realise that all the documents are not being handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know that I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You should know it because you should have applied for a search warrant sometime before March, '97.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, certainly the Prosecution did not, we believe, have sufficient evidence to obtain a search warrant in March of 1997. I would point out that a search warrant in the views of the Prosecution is particularly given the situation in the former Yugoslavia is not something that you go to first because it entails potentially danger for any number of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have not answered the question. When did you realise that all the documents are not being handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour, at various points we believed that all documents were not being handed over to us, but we did not know exactly where those documents were. And, in fact, if you follow the chronology, you can see that some of the documents have followed relatively circuitous routes to get where they were ultimately seized. So the reason we kept making multiple requests is because we believe that there were more documents. And certainly when the Defence counsel started to have documents that we knew that we had not seen before, we certainly renewed our efforts in that regard too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is after you closed your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is with respect to that issue, yes. But I would certainly say before we closed our case, we were continuing from the highest levels of the Office of the Prosecutor to the highest levels of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make sure that we had obtained all documents. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just add a couple of remarks. Regarding certain specific documents, I think that I gave specific arguments, but what my learned colleague has just said is opposite to what they have produced in their written motion. It is clear from it that they had contacted Jasmine Kajunhor (Phoen) as early as '96 and at that she showed them some document. So this was our only on, and the Prosecution should have known and could have known about the existence of a certain document two years ago. And if there was any avoidance, I don't know, there were no search warrant requested. I am not sure whether these documents will produce, possibly, some violence here, I am not going to comment on that. But I believe that the Prosecution did obtain a number of documents and they did so in a very friendly manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what the policies are in regard to search warrants or the practices are in other countries, but I think that in the jurisdiction that I am familiar with, it's been presented that it requires an act of congress or something to get a search warrant. When, in fact, it's been my experience that at least I could say dealing with the United States Department of Justice, they're pretty darn quick to get those things and pretty darn quick to serve them, presuming that they have probable cause. I don't think that it's such a shocking thing to apply for a search warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel was mainly referring to the volatile situation in the jurisdiction at that time. It was not such which you should just apply for search warrant against such functionaries who are dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course search warrants by their very nature can lead to very volatile situations. People that engage, for instance, in the drug trade and search warrants executed on them that there is always a high, high degree danger of violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we'll make our ruling at 2.30 tomorrow afternoon. We shall give a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we close, might I just bring up one matter that is set for tomorrow morning at ten. I believe that last week Mr. Landzo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not aware of any matters tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll just not mention anything more and I'll speak to Mr. Hocking at the close of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose it's a matter not for the Trial Chamber, so you better mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, you do want us in the courtroom tomorrow afternoon, the defendants and us, just for our planning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you said you're going to rule at 2.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Two-thirty tomorrow. Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that will be a session of the Court rather than a written decision being handed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: A decision of the Court. It could be a preliminary ruling and then I give a fuller ruling later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I just wanted to know where I was supposed to be at 2.30 tomorrow

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 3.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of August, 1998, at 2.30 p.m. 25
